sentences.text: This massive dinosaur is estimated to have reached a length of 18 meters and a mass of 15 metric tons.
The humerus of the type specimen measures 134 centimeters in length.
As a large quadrupedal herbivore, an adult held its head 6 meters off the ground.
Postcranial remains previously thought to be lost were later found in the collection of the Geological Survey of India in Calcutta.
The first remains attributed to this animal, a single humerus, were discovered in 1871 or 1872 by Henry Benedict Medlicott.
The holotype remains were found by Charles Alfred Matley between 1917 and 1920 near Jabalpur in the Lameta Formation.
The generic name Jainosaurus honors the Indian paleontologist Sohan Lal Jain, who studied cranial nerve impressions and published results in 1982.
The species was originally named Antarctosaurus septentrionalis by Friedrich von Huene and Matley in 1933.
In 1995, Hunt et al. established the genus Jainosaurus for the species Antarctosaurus septentrionalis, believing it belonged to Dicraeosauridae.
In 2009, Jeffrey Wilson and others confirmed the validity of Jainosaurus septentrionalis after a detailed reassessment.
Wilson and colleagues concluded that Jainosaurus is a valid taxon distinct from Isisaurus.
Jainosaurus belongs to the parent group Lithostrotia.
Jainosaurus lived in India and wider Asia during the Maastrichtian stage, approximately 68 million years ago.
